blocks.text: There are two types of vector multiplications. The product of these two types are known as scalar product and vector product.
If the product of two vectors results in a scalar quantity then it is called scalar product while if the product of two vectors results in a vector quantity then it is called vector product.
Scalar or Dot Product
The scalar product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ is written as A⃗.B⃗ and is defined as

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AB cos θ   (2.6)

blocks.text: where A and B are the magnitudes of vectors A⃗ and B⃗ and θ is the angle between them.
For physical interpretation of dot product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗, these are first brought to a common origin (Fig.2.2 a) then,

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = A (projection of B⃗ on A⃗)

blocks.latex: \text{or}\quad \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A\,(\text{magnitude of component of } \vec{B} \text{ in the direction of } \vec{A}),\ \text{Fig. 2.2(b)}
blocks.text_alt: or A⃗.B⃗ = A (magnitude of component of B⃗ in the direction of A⃗), Fig. 2.2(b)
= A (B cos θ) = AB cos θ
Similarly, B⃗.A⃗ = B (A cos θ) = BA cos θ

blocks.alt: Two panels. (a) Vector A lies along the base; vector B rises at angle theta; a dashed line drops from the tip of B to A, and the shaded piece of A up to that point is labelled B cos theta. (b) The same angle; a dashed line from the tip of A meets B at a right angle, and the piece of B up to that point is labelled A cos theta.
blocks.caption: Dot product: projection of B on A (a) and of A on B (b) (original diagram after Figure 2.2).

blocks.text: We come across this type of product when we consider the work done by a force F⃗ whose point of application moves a distance d in a direction making an angle θ with the line of action of F⃗, as shown in Fig. 2.3.

blocks.latex: \text{Work done} = (\text{Effective component of force in the direction of motion}) \times \text{Distance moved}
blocks.text_alt: Work done = (Effective component of force in the direction of motion) × Distance moved
= (F cos θ) d = Fd cos θ

blocks.text: Using vector notation

blocks.text_alt: F⃗.d⃗ = Fd cos θ = Work done

blocks.alt: A wooden block with a force F pulling from its corner at angle theta above the horizontal. The displacement d points along the horizontal; a dashed line drops from the tip of F to it, and F cos theta marks the part of F along d.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: Work done by a force F at angle θ to the displacement d (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.3).

blocks.text: Characteristics of Scalar Product
1. Since A⃗.B⃗ = AB cosθ and B⃗.A⃗ = BA cos θ = AB cos θ, hence, A⃗.B⃗ = B⃗.A⃗. The order of multiplication is irrelevant. In other words, scalar product is commutative.
2. The scalar product of two mutually perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°) is zero.

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AB cos 90° = 0

blocks.text: 3. The scalar product of two parallel vectors is equal to the product of their magnitudes. Thus for parallel vectors (θ = 0°)

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AB cos 0° = AB

blocks.text: For antiparallel vectors (θ = 180°)

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AB cos 180° = -AB

blocks.text: The self product of a vector A⃗ is equal to square of its magnitude.

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.A⃗ = AA cos 0° = A²

blocks.text: Scalar product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ in terms of their rectangular components

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz   (2.7)

blocks.text: Equation (2.6) can be used to find the angle between two vectors. Since,

blocks.text_alt: A⃗.B⃗ = AB cos θ = AxBx + AyBy + AzBz
Therefore cos θ = (AxBx + AyBy + AzBz)/AB   (2.8)

blocks.text: Vector or Cross Product
The vector product of two vectors A⃗ and B⃗, is a vector which is defined as

blocks.text_alt: A⃗ × B⃗ = AB sin θ n̂   (2.9)

blocks.alt: Vectors A and B lie in a shaded plane with angle theta between them. A x B points straight up from their common tail, perpendicular to the plane; a small arrow beside it marks the unit vector n-hat, and a curled arrow round A x B shows the sense of rotation from A to B.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4(a): The vector product A × B, along n̂ perpendicular to the plane of A and B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.4(a)).

blocks.text: where n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A⃗ and B⃗ as shown in Fig. 2.4 (a). Its direction can be determined by right hand rule. For that purpose, place together the tail of vectors A⃗ and B⃗ to define the plane of vectors A⃗ and B⃗. The direction of the product vector is perpendicular to this plane. Rotate the First vector A⃗ into B⃗ through the smaller of the two possible angles and curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of rotation, keeping the thumb erect. The direction of the product vector will be along the erect thumb, as shown in the Fig 2.4 (b). Because of this direction rule, B⃗ x A⃗ is a vector opposite in sign to A⃗ x B⃗ (Fig. 2.4-c). Hence,

blocks.alt: The same plane with A, B and theta. Above it a right hand with the fingers curled from A towards B and the thumb erect; the thumb points along n-hat, the same way as A x B.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4(b): Right-hand rule for the direction of A × B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.4(b)).

blocks.alt: The plane with A, B and theta, the rotation now from B into A. B x A points straight down from the common tail, opposite to A x B, with a curled arrow round it.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4(c): B × A is opposite to A × B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.4(c)).

blocks.alt: Vectors A and B drawn from one point at angle theta form two sides of a shaded parallelogram; the other two sides are dashed.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.4(d): The parallelogram formed with A and B as adjacent sides (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.4(d)).

blocks.text: Characteristics of Cross Product
1. Since A⃗ x B⃗ is not the same as B⃗ x A⃗, the cross product is non commutative. so,
2. The cross product of two perpendicular vectors (θ = 90°) has maximum magnitude

blocks.text_alt: A⃗ × B⃗ = AB sin 90° n̂ = AB n̂

blocks.text: 3. The cross product of two parallel vectors is null vector, because for such vectors θ = 0° or 180°, Hence,

blocks.text_alt: A⃗ × B⃗ = AB sin 0° n̂ = 0 or A⃗ × B⃗ = AB sin 180° n̂ = 0

blocks.text: As a consequence A⃗ x A⃗ = 0 (θ = 0°)
4. The magnitude of A⃗ x B⃗ is equal to the area of the parallelogram formed with A⃗ and B⃗ as two adjacent sides Fig.2.4 (d).
Examples of Vector Product

i. When a force F⃗ is applied on a rigid body at a point whose position vector is r from any point on the axis about which the body rotates, then the turning effect of the force called the torque τ is given by the vector product of r⃗ and F⃗.
ii. The force F⃗ on a particle of charge q and velocity v⃗ in a magnetic field of strength B⃗ is given by vector product of v⃗ and B⃗.
